title: The Ways a Package Fills a Fresh Instance
appliesTo: nothing to look at after the install
hints: Core reads four things out of a package at typo3 extension:setup, and in each case the file being there is the whole declaration: Initialisation/data.t3d or Initialisation/data.xml for the page tree and the content, Initialisation/Site/<identifier>/ for the site configuration, Initialisation/Files/ for what is copied into fileadmin under the extension key, and ext_tables_static+adt.sql for static table rows. sitepackage-initial-content is the first two of those and initial-content-import-once is why a second setup imports nothing.

The static SQL file is the one that does arrive again: the registry keeps its hash rather than a flag, so an edited ext_tables_static+adt.sql is imported on the next setup while an edited data file is not.

hints.text: A package can fill the instance itself instead, by listening on the package initialization event — the same event every import above is a listener on, so a listener of its own runs at extension:setup with no file convention behind it.

hints: A console command the package ships is a declaration a caller can see and core never runs: it is tagged console.command and it stands in typo3 list, and what fills the instance is somebody typing it.

hints.text: A site set fills nothing by itself. Configuration/Sets/<name>/config.yaml carries TypoScript, page TSconfig, settings and labels, and it reaches an installation only where a site's own config.yaml names it under dependencies — so a package shipping sets alone needs a site to exist before any of it applies.

hints: A package declaring none of them still fills the instance, by a procedure only its own manual writes down — a backend module to click through, or steps to follow by hand. Nothing the package registers says which module that is, so the manual is the source rather than the file listing, and the absence of everything above is what says to read it.

title: Shipping Initial Content with an Extension
hints: An extension ships content as Initialisation/data.t3d or Initialisation/data.xml. It is imported once, when the package is set up — typo3 extension:setup is what triggers it. Initialisation/Site/<identifier>/ ships the site configuration alongside it, and Initialisation/Files/ is copied into the fileadmin directory under the extension key.

typo3 setup and typo3 extension:setup are two commands, and the second one is where the content arrives: it fires the package initialization. An extension whose shipped content changed afterwards is set up with that command on its own.

hints.text: The setup command runs the extension setup as its last step, so a first install does both.

An extension that ships one of those files is a distribution as far as the setup command is concerned: the presence of the file is the entire test. So when such a package is already active, setup skips its own site creation and says that --distribution and --create-site have no effect; the two options exclude each other in any case, and --distribution needs typo3/cms-impexp to be active before it is offered at all.
The setup dispatches a package initialization event, and every import — the content, the site configurations, the static SQL — is a listener on it, so an extension can add its own.

hints: initial-content-import-once is why a changed file does not arrive: the import runs once and the registry remembers it, so nothing reaches an installation that already ran it. initial-content-references is what survives the import, and it is where shipped content ends up pointing at a stranger's records and the seeded site answers HTTP 404 at its own root. impexp-artifact writes the file in the first place, and the export it writes answers [OK] with the images left out. fresh-instance-seeding is the other ways a package fills an instance, for a package that ships no such file at all.

title: Why a Changed Data File Does Not Arrive
hints: The import runs exactly once and remembers that in the registry, namespace extensionDataImport. A second setup imports nothing, which is the point — and also why a changed data file does not reach an installation that already ran it. Deleting that one sys_registry row is what makes extension:setup import the file again.

hints.text: The key is <extension_key>:Initialisation/dataImported, and <extension_key>:Initialisation/data.t3d blocks the import just as well, because both are checked.

The key is the extension's path below the public directory with Initialisation/dataImported appended — typo3conf/ext/<extension_key>/Initialisation/dataImported for an extension installed there — and the sibling ending in Initialisation/data.t3d blocks the import just as well, because both are checked.

hints: So the file is write-only on the installation it was exported from: whoever maintains it cannot see the effect of their own change there, and reading the XML back is reasoning rather than verification. Import it where it can be imported — a functional test is the cheap form: get(Import::class), loadFile('EXT:<key>/Initialisation/data.xml'), importData(), then assert the records arrived. typo3/sysext/impexp/Tests/Functional/ImportTest.php is the worked example.

title: What Survives the Import, and What Points at a Stranger
hints: What survives the import is what the reference index sees. The export gathers relations with ReferenceIndex::getRelations(), so a uid is remapped where TCA declares the field as a relation, or where a soft reference parser finds it — a type=link field ships as a typolink soft reference with the record it points at, a type=group to pages as a database relation, inside a FlexForm as well. The same page uid in a plain input or number field is exported as the integer it is and imported as that integer, pointing at whatever the target installation has under it. Nothing warns, so the field type is what decides whether shipped content survives.

The Initialisation/Site/ route remaps the root page id to the page that was actually imported, and nothing else. Every other reference in the shipped config.yaml — an error handler naming t3://page?uid=..., a redirect target — keeps the uid it was exported with, so it points at a stranger's record on the second installation. Ship a site configuration with no uid in it but the root page; where one is unavoidable, the configuration is good for a first install and nothing else, and the extension says so where someone will read it.

A site identifier that already exists in Initialisation/Site/ is skipped with a warning, so a fresh installation and an existing one behave differently. Creating a site during setup and shipping one in Initialisation/Site/ are alternatives, not steps: the first one leaves a site behind that makes the second one be skipped.

hints.text: A site configuration carried inside the export file itself takes the other route and loses its base: Import::processSiteConfigurations() overwrites base with /<identifier>/ and discards the exported value, because the importer cannot know the target installation's domain. So an installation seeded from a distribution by typo3 extension:setup answers HTTP 404 at the project root and is reachable only under /<identifier>/, until base in config/sites/<identifier>/config.yaml is corrected by hand or in the backend. There is no event and no option on that rewrite, and where the identifier is already taken it is suffixed with -1 and the base follows the suffix.

Two conditions stop that method running at all, and both read like the cause: an importing backend user who is not an admin, in which case no site configuration arrives, and a package shipping Initialisation/Site/, where ImportSiteConfigurationsOnPackageInitialization takes over and the shipped base survives untouched.

hints: site-base-collision is another cause of an HTTP 404 at the project root and the one to check where nothing was imported: a bare path loses every request to a site naming the host, so the answer comes out of the wrong site's page tree. autogenerated-site-configuration is the one to check where the site identifier reads autogenerated-<uid>-<md5 of that uid>: the core wrote that site when a root page was created, and the hook writing it returns early while an import is running, so a site named that way is never what an import left behind.

title: Writing the Export a Distribution Ships
hints: The import lives in EXT:impexp, so an extension that ships content has to require typo3/cms-impexp.

hints.text: Without it the requirement check only logs a warning: the setup succeeds and the installation comes up empty, which is far harder to notice than a failure.

hints: Once content exists, the console's impexp export writes the artifact and impexp import reads it back — which is also the way in for the first build, where there is nothing to export yet and hand-writing T3D is not an option: seed with DataHandler, then export.
impexp:export takes one --table per table, and a custom table nobody named is missing from the export without a word: typo3 impexp:export --table=tt_content --table=tx_myext_product.

Images do not come along with the reference: --include-related=sys_file is what admits the sys_file record, and the bytes hang off that record rather than off the sys_file_reference. Naming sys_file under --table admits nothing, because a page tree holds no sys_file rows. The reference table still has to be named as well, under --table or under --include-related, and --include-related=sys_file_metadata is what brings the alt texts and titles with it.

Where the bytes then go is --save-files-outside-export-file: beside the export instead of base64 inside it, into a directory named after the file plus .files, each under its own sha1. That is the shape for an artifact that is committed. The import picks that directory up whenever it sits next to the file, extension:setup included, and reuses a file the target storage already has under the same identifier and hash rather than duplicating it.

The export keeps the basename of the filename argument and drops the rest: EXT:my_package/Initialisation/data becomes data, and the file lands in the default import-export folder below fileadmin. Nothing rejects the path that was dropped, and the success message names where the file went. A package artifact is moved into place afterwards, its .files directory with it. EXT:<key>/Initialisation/data.xml is the form that works for impexp:import, which resolves its argument through GeneralUtility::getFileAbsFileName().

impexp:export answers [OK] whatever it left out, so the artifact is what says whether it worked. A correct one has a files_fal section beside header and records, and its .files directory holds one file per image.
impexp-import-placement is the other half, for a file being read back rather than written: what decides the page an imported record lands on.

title: Where an impexp Import Puts the Records It Writes
appliesTo: imported page on the wrong pid
imported records landed on the import target
imported translations on the wrong page
import moved the page tree flat
hints: Import::writePages() decides the page: it takes each page's pid out of header.records.pages, maps it through importNewIdPids, and falls back to the import target where that lookup misses. addSingle() fills the map as each page is added, so the write order is what decides whether a parent resolves at all. A page reached before its parent lands on the import target rather than in the tree, and nothing reports it.

header.pagetree is read as a tree by the import and appended to as a flat marker set by the export. Export writes every page translation into it under its own uid, so the record counts as inside the page tree; ImportExport::flatInversePageTree() reads the same section as a real tree, reverses each level and hands every top level node the pid -1. The appended nodes come out of it first, carrying that -1 into the lookup above.

addSingle() sets a pid only for a record it creates. Where the record maps onto an existing uid it unsets pid instead, so an update cannot move a page through the datamap — which is what writePagesOrder() is for, a correction pass that moves the written pages with a cmdmap afterwards.

That pass is narrower than it looks: writePagesOrder() returns unless the import is an update, and its move is guarded by $pagePid >= 0, so every node carrying -1 is outside it as well. A record the fallback placed on the import target stays there.

impexp:import --update-records is what turns update mode on: records with a matching uid are updated in place instead of inserted, and the correction pass runs. --ignore-pid turns that pass off again through doRespectPid() and works only together with --update-records. The same switch per record is --import-mode "<table>:<uid>=ignore_pid", against which =respect_pid is the exception.
initial-content-references is the other reason an imported record points somewhere unexpected: which relations survive the import at all.
